text: Given an array of size n, return the majority element — the one that appears more than n over two times, rounded down. You may assume it always exists. Follow-up: can you do it in linear time and constant space?

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — majority means strictly more than half, and it's guaranteed to exist, so I don't need to handle the no-majority case. That also means the array is never empty. And the follow-up wants both linear time and constant space. Is that right?

Let me run through the example. Two, two, one, one, one, two, two gives two, since two appears four times, and four is more than seven over two. Notice the twos are split into two separate runs, so I can't just look at neighbors. That matches.

Let me think about the space constraint. A naive approach would count with a hash map — linear time, but linear space too. Sorting and taking the middle element is n log n. To hit linear time and constant space, I need something smarter than counting everything. This problem reminds me of the Boyer-Moore voting algorithm, a cancellation pattern, and it fits because the majority outnumbers everyone else combined. The intuition: pair up two different elements and cancel them. Since the majority can't be fully cancelled, whatever survives is the answer.
How do you simulate that cancelling with constant space?

Keep a candidate and a count. For each element: if the count is zero, adopt this element as the candidate with count one; if it equals the candidate, increment — that's reinforcing; otherwise decrement — an opposing vote cancels one. The key point is that count isn't the candidate's true frequency. It's how far ahead the current candidate is. When it hits zero, the lead is wiped out, and the next element starts fresh.

Here's the plan. One: start with count zero. Two: for each number, adopt it when count is zero, add one when it matches the candidate, subtract one when it doesn't. Three: return the candidate. Since existence is guaranteed, one pass is enough — no verification needed. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Two scalars, count and candidate, and one loop with three exclusive branches: adopt, reinforce, or cancel. Then I return the candidate. One thing worth flagging — the count-is-zero check has to come first, and the branches are an if, else-if chain. A freshly adopted element starts at one; it must not fall through and get compared again in the same step. Also, the starting candidate of zero is just a placeholder — the first element always replaces it. That's linear time and constant space, with two scalars and one pass.

Then this candidate is only the one that survived — not necessarily a true majority. Boyer-Moore guarantees that if a majority exists, it must be this candidate, but it can't prove that one exists. So I'd add a second pass, counting the candidate's actual occurrences, and return it only if that count is more than n over two; otherwise, report none. That's still linear time and constant space. Here existence is promised, so I skip it.

Let's dry-run the code on two, two, one, one, one, two, two — I picked it because the candidate flips. Expected two. The row that matters is the sixth element: that two cancels the one-candidate's lead down to zero, so the last two gets adopted and ends as the candidate. The candidate went two, one, two — but the true majority can't be held down, so it wins. Corner cases: three, two, three gives three; a single element returns itself; a majority that only shows up at the end still wins. I also verified against a hash-count reference on eight thousand random arrays, each built with a real majority — zero mismatches.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear, space is constant — exactly the follow-up. There's no early exit, so every case reads each element exactly once. Oh, one more thing — it generalizes nicely. For elements that appear more than n over three times, there can be at most two, so you run Boyer-Moore with two candidates and two counters, decrementing both on an unmatched vote. There, the verification pass becomes mandatory. And because it keeps only constant state and never looks back, it's a genuine single-pass streaming algorithm — you could run it over a data stream too large to store.

Excellent. Three things stood out. You reached the constant-space bar with Boyer-Moore, and explained why cancellation forces the majority to survive. You knew that count is a lead, not a frequency, which is the part people usually get wrong. And you knew when the verification pass is required. Strong.
